title: X2 · 3 a.m.: the WAL that wouldn’t stop growing
description: orders-db is paging. Redraw the write path from memory, then name the step that stopped. Three hearts, and every wrong submit costs one.

problemStatement.overview:
**03:07. You’re on call.** PagerDuty fires: `orders-db disk /data/wal 41 GB (normal < 1 GB)`.

You open the dashboard:

- `/data/wal` has been climbing in a straight line since **01:52**.
- `sstable_count` has been flat at **212** since 01:52.
- `immutable_memtables` is **3 of 4**. RocksDB will stall all writes at 4.
- `p99 PUT latency` still looks fine, **for now**.

Arjun, the incident lead, joins the call: *"Before anyone restarts anything, draw me how a write is supposed to flow. Then tell me which step stopped at 01:52."*

You have **three hearts**. Every Submit with a wrong board costs one. Finish with all three for three stars.
problemStatement.yourTask: Rebuild the write path, then answer Arjun: which step stopped?
yourTaskSteps: Place six cards on the write path. One optional card exists.
Submit. A wrong board costs a heart.
When the board is right, answer the final question. A wrong answer also costs a heart.
hints: WAL segments are deleted only after something else finishes. What?
If the SSTable count is flat, files aren’t being created.
problemStatement.moat: Classic board with lives=3 and finale answer = flush.

platformSpec.passMessage: Found it. Flushes stopped at 01:52, so WAL segments couldn’t be deleted.

finale.prompt: Arjun: “OK, the board’s right. So which step stopped at 01:52?”
finale.explanation: The SSTable count is flat, so no flush has finished since 01:52. Frozen memtables are piling up (3 of 4), and WAL segments can only be deleted after their memtable is flushed, which is why the WAL grows. Deleting WAL segments is a symptom, not the cause. A compaction stall wouldn’t make the WAL grow.

pieces.title: Append to the WAL and fsync
pieces.blurb: Every PUT lands at the end of the current WAL segment in /data/wal first.

pieces.title: Insert into the active memtable
pieces.blurb: The record joins the in-memory sorted tree and the client gets its OK.

pieces.title: Freeze the full memtable
pieces.blurb: At 64 MB the memtable becomes immutable and a new one (with a new WAL segment) takes writes. This is what immutable_memtables counts.

pieces.title: Flush the frozen memtable to a new SSTable
pieces.blurb: A background thread writes it to /data/sst as a new file. This is what makes sstable_count go up.

pieces.title: Write a Bloom filter and index
pieces.blurb: Optional read speed-up stored next to the new SSTable.

pieces.title: Delete the WAL segment for that memtable
pieces.blurb: Only safe once its memtable is in an SSTable. This is what keeps /data/wal small.

pieces.title: Compaction merges SSTables
pieces.blurb: Background merge-sort of older files into fewer, larger ones.

pieces.title: Overwrite the order’s page on disk
pieces.blurb: Go to the page holding order:88213 and write the new value over it.
pieces.trapIfPlaced: That’s a B-tree. LSM engines never overwrite in place.

pieces.title: Truncate the WAL when the disk alert fires
pieces.blurb: If /data/wal passes 40 GB, chop the oldest segments to free space.
pieces.trapIfPlaced: Those segments hold records that aren’t in any SSTable yet. Truncating them loses data on the next crash.

pieces.title: Reply OK first, write the log later
pieces.blurb: Batch WAL writes every second for lower latency.
pieces.trapIfPlaced: A crash in that second loses acknowledged orders.

pieces.title: Delete old versions from every SSTable right away
pieces.blurb: Edit each SSTable that holds an older version of the key.
pieces.trapIfPlaced: SSTables are immutable. Old versions wait for compaction.

pieces.title: Pause writes during compaction
pieces.blurb: Writes wait until the merge finishes.
pieces.trapIfPlaced: Compaction runs in the background. Writes don’t wait for it.
